claims.statement: Five hundred thousand dollars a year. For a rookie who had never played a single NBA game.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'Nike offered Jordan $500,000 a year in cash for five years'. The pitch came after the summer 1984 Olympics, before his NBA debut (N1).

claims.statement: About three times the best shoe deal around / Nike is about to smash the record.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'The previous highest contract was James Worthy's deal with New Balance, an eight-year deal worth $150,000 a year.' Wikipedia: 'three times more than any other deal in the NBA at the time.'

claims.statement: From a company that had just lost money / Nike posted its first quarterly loss. Ever. (February)
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013 (re-opened in round 2): 'In February 1984, the company reported its first quarterly loss ever.'

claims.statement: Under thirty million in sales in 1973; $867M by the end of '83; yearly sales about $867M.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013 (re-opened): 'revenue went from $28.7 million in 1973 to $867 million by the end of 1983.'

claims.statement: It's been a public company since 1980.
claims.evidence: Knight, 2004 letter: 'When we went public in 1980, we had 7,500 original investors.'

claims.statement: Even in its rough year, Nike still made over forty million in profit.
claims.evidence: Knight quoting his 1984 letter: 'In fiscal year 1984, we made over $40 million in net income'.

claims.statement: Reebok coming up fast; by the mid-eighties Reebok passed Nike as America's biggest athletic shoe maker; by 1988 it had lost that top spot.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing WSJ 2005): Reebok 'overtook Nike ... as the largest athletic shoe manufacturer in the US before losing the top position in 1988.'

claims.statement: Since 1977, Vaccaro has signed about eighty college coaches.
claims.evidence: USA Today 2015 (re-opened): 'Vaccaro joined Nike in 1977 ... signing endorsement deals with about 80 coaches'.

claims.statement: College player of the year. The Chicago Bulls take him third in the draft, on June 19.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2016 (re-opened), Falk: 'He was the national player of the year.' 3rd pick on June 19, 1984 per research s10 (undisputed).

claims.statement: He wore Converse in college. He wanted Adidas. He had never even worn a pair (of Nikes).
claims.evidence: ESPN 2016: 'Jordan wore Converse in college and preferred Adidas.' USA Today 2015 (re-opened), Jordan: 'In all honesty, I never wore Nike shoes until I signed with Nike.'

claims.statement: Phil Knight, co-founder and boss; Rob Strasser, the marketing chief; agent David Falk.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'Nike president and co-founder Phil Knight'. ESPN 2016: '[marketing head] Rob Strasser'; Falk 'represented Jordan in contract and marketing negotiations'.

claims.statement: Converse is offering him about a hundred thousand dollars a year.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'a financial package of about $100,000 a year'. ESPN 2016: 'Converse offered $100,000 per year.'

claims.statement: Five hundred thousand a year. For five years. About two and a half million dollars in cash.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013 and 2016 (both re-opened): $500,000 a year for five years. Wikipedia says six years, $2.5M; script follows the majority.

claims.statement: Add stock options, and by Falk's count the package could reach about seven million.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'Adding stock options and other parts of the deal, Falk said Jordan would earn $7 million over those five years'. Attributed.

claims.statement: According to ESPN's reporting, Spot-Bilt bid more (Nike's offer wasn't the biggest in cash).
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'In straight-up cash, Spot-Bilt's deal would be worth more than what Nike offered.' ESPN 2016: Spot-Bilt 'submitted the highest bid, including Nike.'

claims.statement: His own shoe line. His name on it. And royalties: a cut of the sales.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: signature shoe line; 'Jordan would get royalties from products sold by Nike with his name.' Jordan (USA Today): Strasser presented 'the Air Jordan concept'.

claims.statement: By Falk's account, a million dollars of marketing in the first six months.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013 (re-opened): Falk 'said he made them commit to putting $1 million into marketing Jordan's shoes in their first six months on the shelves.'

claims.statement: Jordan's fee was less than a tenth of one percent of $867M.
According to Falk, an escape hatch: miss Rookie of the Year, All-Star, 20 ppg in his first three years and Nike could walk away two years early.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013 (re-opened): 'if he didn't accomplish one of three things -- win Rookie of the Year, become an All-Star or average 20 points per game -- in his first three years, it could end the deal two years early.' Attributed to Falk.

claims.statement: Jordan didn't want to go. His parents talked him into it.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'I have no interest in going there'; Falk called James and Deloris. Jordan (USA Today): 'my parents made me go out'.

claims.statement: At Nike's HQ in Oregon: highlight tape to the Pointer Sisters' 'Jump'; a shoe built around him; by Falk's telling Strasser pulled out two toy Mercedes cars.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013 (re-opened): Beaverton, Ore.; 'highlight tape of himself to the Pointer Sisters "Jump"'; Moore 'could tailor them to Jordan's liking'; 'Strasser reached in and took out two die-cast Mercedes cars.'

claims.statement: "I was very loyal," Jordan said, as quoted by ESPN. He took Nike's offer back to Adidas and said: "This is the Nike contract, if you come anywhere close, I'll sign with you guys."
claims.evidence: Round-1 fix applied. ESPN 2013 (re-opened): '"I was very loyal," Jordan said at the time. "I went back to my adidas contract and said, 'This is the Nike contract -- if you come anywhere close, I'll sign with you guys.'"' Attribution and wording now match.

claims.statement: According to ESPN's reporting, Adidas had shown almost no interest. And Adidas didn't come close.
claims.evidence: Round-1 fix applied. ESPN 2016 (re-opened), reporter's voice: 'By all accounts, Adidas had almost no interest in Jordan'. ESPN 2013: 'adidas wasn't making an offer' and, after Jordan's last pitch, 'It wasn't happening.'

claims.statement: That fall, Michael Jordan signed with Nike.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'On October 26, 1984, Jordan signed...'. USA Today: deal 'consummated in 1984'. 'That fall' is safely vague.

claims.statement: The NBA banned his red and black Nike shoes. The reported fine: five thousand dollars a game. Nike could have backed down. Instead, by most accounts, it paid.
claims.evidence: Slate 2023 (re-opened): Granik letter prohibiting 'certain red and black Nike basketball shoes' around Oct 18, 1984; the game shoe was likely the Air Ship. Wikipedia: '$5,000 fine per game ... Nike agreed to pay each fine.' ESPN 2013: 'Nike paid the fines'. Optional hedge 'by most accounts' applied.

claims.statement: Ad punchline: "Fortunately, the NBA can't keep you from wearing them."
claims.evidence: Slate 2023 (re-opened): 'Fortunately, the N.B.A. can't keep you from wearing them'. Also in ESPN 2013.

claims.statement: Air Jordan One hit stores in spring 1985. $65 a pair. Goal: $3M over three years.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: '$65 a pair, hit stores nationwide in March 1985'. Wikipedia: released April 1985 'with the goal of making $3 million in the first three years.'

claims.statement: By May, seventy million dollars' worth. By the end of the first year, more than a hundred million. More than thirty times the goal, in a third of the time.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'By May, Nike had sold $70 million worth. By year's end ... more than $100 million in revenues.' ESPN 2016 (re-opened): '$70 million worth of Air Jordans in its first two months on sale in 1985.' $100M / $3M = 33x.

claims.statement: Escape hatch never needed. Jordan was Rookie of the Year. He made the All-Star team.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'won the Rookie of the Year award'. 1985 All-Star selection per research s10 (undisputed).

claims.statement: In 1997, Jordan became a brand of its own.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In 1997, Jordan and Nike introduced Jordan Brand (originally called "Brand Jordan").'

claims.statement: In 2022 alone, Jordan Brand brought in five point one billion. About two thousand times the whole cash deal.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In 2022 alone, Jordan Brand brought in $5.1 billion to Nike.' $5.1B / $2.5M = 2,040x (about 1,700x at six years/$3M; 'about two thousand' holds).

claims.statement: Today, that bet brings in more than five billion dollars a year.
claims.evidence: Nike FY2026 earnings release (SEC exhibit 99.1): Jordan Brand sales '$7,034 million in fiscal 2026 compared to $7,270 million in fiscal 2025.'

claims.statement: Jordan's reported Nike earnings that year: $150 to $256 million.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'a reported $150–256 million went directly to Jordan under his royalties deal with Nike.' Stated as a reported range.

claims.statement: Nike as a whole: from $867M to $46.4B in fiscal 2026. About fifty times bigger.
claims.evidence: Nike FY2026 release: 'Full year revenues were $46.4 billion'. $46,398M / $867M = 53.5x.

claims.statement: Jordan: "Would the brand have been as strong if it was adidas? We'll never know."
claims.evidence: Verbatim in ESPN 2013 (round 1).

claims.statement: Vaccaro says he picked Jordan and urged Nike to spend its whole allotted budget on him. Knight and Jordan dispute his role. The 2023 movie goes further: Vaccaro bets his job, and the whole basketball division, on one rookie. For that version, we found no source beyond Vaccaro's own account.
claims.evidence: Round-1 fix applied verbatim. USA Today 2015 (re-opened): Vaccaro 'urged Nike to spend all of its allotted budget to sign Jordan'; Knight: 'Sonny helped, but he wasn't the MVP'; Jordan: 'it really wasn't Sonny'. ESPN 2016, Vaccaro: 'I picked him'. Slate 2023: in the film Vaccaro bets 'not only his job but the entire basketball division on the deal'. Attributed and hedged correctly.

claims.statement: Knight credits Strasser and Moore; "Sonny helped, but he wasn't the MVP in that process." Jordan credits Strasser and George Raveling.
claims.evidence: USA Today 2015 (re-opened), verbatim. Knight: MVPs were Strasser and Moore. Jordan: 'it was actually George Raveling'; 'I absolutely fell in love with (Strasser)'.

claims.statement: Vaccaro was fired by Nike in 1991. Knight: "Success has a thousand fathers and failure is an orphan."
claims.evidence: USA Today 2015 (re-opened): 'fired by Nike in 1991 without public explanation'; Knight: 'success has a thousand fathers and failure is an orphan' (verbatim).

notes: Round 2 (script v2). All three round-1 issues are fixed exactly as asked, and the optional hedge ('by most accounts, it paid') was also applied. I re-opened ESPN 2013, ESPN 2016, USA Today 2015 and Slate 2023 and checked the changed sentences word for word: the Q2 attribution now matches 'Jordan said at the time'; the Adidas line is now credited to ESPN's own reporting ('By all accounts'); the credit-fight passage now matches USA Today (Vaccaro's 'all of its allotted budget') and Slate (in the film, Vaccaro bets his job and the basketball division). I compared the rest of the script with v1, and the round-1 results still hold (35/38 ok then). All 38 statements are now ok, with no unsupported, wrong or unflagged disputed items. All five quotes are verbatim and properly attributed. The figures are the conservative ones and no inflation-adjusted values are used. Hindsight fairness is strong. Structure: the freeze comes at about 4:23 of about 8:47 (50%), followed by the reveal, the numbers, the verdict 'Signed.' and one lesson. About 1,305 words fits the long format. Ready for @director.
